heroHeadline: S&P 500 Closes May at Record 7,580 (+5%); China NBS PMI Falls to Borderline 50.0 (New Orders in Contraction 49.9); Chicago PMI Surges to 4-Year High 62.7; Iran MOU 'Mostly Agreed' But Unsigned Through Weekend; Warsh '3 Reforms' Outlined — Balance Sheet, Forward Guidance, Inflation Gauge; Section 122 Cliff 53 Days
heroSubtitle: The global recession risk landscape as of May 31, 2026 — Day 17 of the Warsh Fed era — is defined by a striking divergence: US equity markets and domestic manufacturing are surging while Chinese demand is stalling at the borderline, Iran deal diplomacy drags on unsigned, and the Warsh Fed is preparing three structural reforms that could materially reshape global borrowing costs. On the equity and manufacturing side, the S&P 500 closed May at a record 7,580.06 — up 5% for the month — while the Chicago PMI surged to 62.7, a 4-year high and the largest monthly jump since 2020, implying the ISM Manufacturing index (due June 1) could print above 50 for the first time since September 2022. Brent crude fell approximately 19% for the full month of May 2026 to approximately $92.56/bbl — the largest monthly oil price decline since the COVID demand collapse of April 2020 — driven by tentative Iran deal progress. However, as of May 31, the 60-day Memorandum of Understanding drafted by US and Iranian negotiators remains unsigned: diplomatic sources describe it as 'mostly agreed,' but President Trump has not endorsed it, Vice President Vance cited 'a couple of language points still being discussed,' and the White House has previously denied Iranian claims of a finalized deal. The US military remains on 'ready to resume combat' posture in the Gulf. On the China side, the National Bureau of Statistics released the May 2026 Manufacturing PMI at exactly 50.0 — the statistical boundary between expansion and contraction — with the new orders sub-index slipping to 49.9, the first contraction reading in three months. This signals that the front-loading-driven Q1 2026 GDP beat of 5.0% is now fading, with Q2 momentum stalling under dual headwinds from Iran war Middle East demand destruction and the US-China 31.6% effective tariff barrier; a PBOC counter-cyclical response is widely expected. The most consequential new development is the detailed emergence of Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's three structural reform pillars (per Philadelphia Inquirer and Motley Fool analyses on May 31, Day 17): first, acceleration of quantitative tightening beyond Powell's pace toward a $4-5T balance sheet target from the current $6.7T — which would structurally elevate 10Y+ yields and pressure equity valuations via higher discount rates; second, elimination of forward guidance and calendar-based rate commitments in favor of meeting-by-meeting assessment using the overnight repo market as a real-time financial conditions signal — a 'real regime change in Wall Street's plumbing'; and third, shifting the primary inflation gauge from the headline PCE (which Warsh has called a 'rough swag') to the Dallas Fed trimmed-mean PCE and Cleveland Fed median CPI, which both show a more favorable trajectory. Warsh's June 16-17 FOMC — his first as Chair, coinciding with the Bank of Japan's June 16 meeting where a rate hike to 1.00% is priced at 65-77% probability — remains the highest-stakes single-day concentration of global monetary policy risk in 2026. The five-step critical path now stands: June 1 (ISM Manufacturing + Caixin China PMI) → June 5 (Iran MOU signature window + May jobs report) → June 16 (BOJ hike + Warsh inaugural FOMC) → July 24 (Section 122 tariff cliff, 53 days). Goldman Sachs: 30% US recession probability; JPMorgan: 35%; Moody's Analytics: 49%.
